                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>BUT it came to pass within a while after, in the time of wheat harvest <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which circumstance is noted as the proper season for the following exploit.</ns0:note>, that Samson vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sited his wife with a kid: and he said, I will go in to my wife into the chamber <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Into her proper Chamber, which Women had distinct and separate from the mens.</ns0:note>. But her fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther would not suffer him to go in.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And her father said, I verily thought that thou hadst utterly hated her <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Because thou didst desert her in great Wrath: But this was not sufficient cause; for he should have endeavoured a reconciliation, or waited for it; and not have disposed of another mans Wife without his consent, which is not onely against the Law of God, but of Nature also.</ns0:note>, therefore I gave her to thy companion: <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not her younger sister fairer than she? <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Let her be thine.</ns0:note> take her, I pray thee, instead of her.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 ¶ And Samson said concerning them, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> shall I be blameless. from the <ns0:hi>Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines</ns0:hi> thirst.</ns0:note> Now shall I be more blameless than the Philistines, though I do them a displeasure <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Because they have first provoked me by an irreparable injury: But although this may look like an act of private revenge; yet it is plain enough, that <ns0:hi>Samson</ns0:hi> acted as a judge (for so he was) and as an avenger of the publick Injuries and Oppressions of his People, as plainly appears from hence, that <ns0:hi>Samson</ns0:hi> designed this very thing before he had received any personal injury, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 14. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And Samson went and caught three hundred foxes <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Of which there were great numbers in <ns0:hi>Canaan,</ns0:hi> as appears from <ns0:hi>Neh.</ns0:hi> 4. 3. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 62. 11. <ns0:hi>Cant<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>c.</ns0:hi> 2. 15. <ns0:hi>Lam.</ns0:hi> 5. 18. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 13. 4. So that divers places there have their Names from the Foxes which abounded there; as, <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 15. 28. and 19. 42. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 13. 17. Add to this, that some Learned men concieve that the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Name <ns0:hi>Schual</ns0:hi> is more general, and contains not only the Foxes, but ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther sort of Creature very like to them, called <ns0:hi>Thoes,</ns0:hi> whereof there were so many there, that sometimes 200 of them have been met together in one Company; as some who have lived in those parts have left upon Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cord: But Infidels are much scandalized at this History, and pretend it incredible that <ns0:hi>Samson</ns0:hi> should catch so many Fox<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />es together; so nice and delicate is the Faith of these men in things concerning God and Scripture, that can devour things ten times more difficult and absurd, concerning the production of the World, and of men<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But there is no cause of wonder here, for any man that is tollerably wi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e; for it is not said that <ns0:hi>Samson</ns0:hi> caught them all, either at one time, or by his own hands; for being so eminent a per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, and the Judge of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> he might require assistance of as many persons as he pleased, and all his people would readily assist him; nor can it at all perplex any mans Reason or Faith, if it be allowed, that the God who made the World, and by his singular Providence watched over <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and intended them deliverance at this time, could easily dispose things so that they might be taken. He chose to do this exploit, not by his Brethren, whom he would preserve from the Envy, and Hatred, and Mischief which that might have occasioned to them, but by bruit Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, thereby to add scorn and contempt to their Cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity, and particularly by Foxes; partly, because they were fittest for the purpose, being Creatures very fearful of Fire; and having such Tails as the Fire-brands might most con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />veniently be tied to; and not going directly forward, but croo<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>edly and involvedly, whereby the Fire was likely to be dispersed in more places.</ns0:note>, and took <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Torches.</ns0:note> fire-brands <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Made of such matter as would quickly take Fire, and keep it for a long time, which was easy to procure.</ns0:note>, and turned tail to tail, and put a fire-brand in the midst between two tails <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">That the Foxes might not make too much haste, nor run into their holes, but one of them might delay and stop another in his course, and so continue longer in the places where they were to do Execution.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And when he had set the brands on fire, he let <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> go <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To wit, successively at several times; and in divers pla<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, with great care and discretion, so as they might no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> hinder one another, nor all run into the same Field; but being dispersed in all parts, might spread the Plague far<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther; and withal might be kept at a distance from the Fields and Vineyards of the <ns0:hi>Israelites.</ns0:hi> It is not worthy of our enqui<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>y what became of these Foxes afterward, whether they were burnt by the Fire-brands, or run into Holes, or were taken and killed by the <ns0:hi>Philistines.</ns0:hi> The truth of this History is notably attested by a custom of the <ns0:hi>Romans,</ns0:hi> which it is very probable they had from the <ns0:hi>Phoenicians,</ns0:hi> upon this occasion; for every year they had a Solemnity in <ns0:hi>April,</ns0:hi> the very time of <ns0:hi>Canaan</ns0:hi>'s Wheat-Har<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vest, wherein Foxes were let loose with burning Torches fastned to their Back-sides, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> into the standing corn of the Phili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stines, and burnt up both the shocks, and also the standing corn, with the vineyards <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> olives.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 ¶ Then the Philistines said, Who hath done this? and they answered, Samson the son in law of the Timnite, because he had taken his wife, and given her to his companion. And the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listins came up and burnt her <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Partly, for her Adultery, which divers Heathens punish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed with Death; and partly, for that mischief which she had occasioned to them; thus she brought upon her self that mischief which she studied to avoid, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 14. 15. as wicked persons oft do, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 10. 24.</ns0:note> and her father with fire.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 ¶ And Samson said unto them, Though ye have done this, yet will I be avenged of you <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whereby it appears, that it was not his private inju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ries, but the Publick, which he did revenge.</ns0:note>, and after that I will cease.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 And he smote them hip and thigh <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Upon their Hips and Thighs, peradventure not designing to Kill them, but to make them uncapable of Military em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployment; or, of doing hurt to the <ns0:hi>Israelites.</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>He smote them with his Leg upon their Thigh,</ns0:hi> i. e. without any other Weapon but his Leg and Foot he kicked them, and made them Lame and useless for War.</ns0:note> with a great slaughter <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>with a great stroke;</ns0:hi> for so it was, even to them whom it did not Kill.</ns0:note>; and he went down and dwelt in the top of the rock Etam <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Partly, because there he could better defend him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self from his Enemies; and partly, because he would not involve his Brethren in the same danger with himself, but like a Worthy Magistrate, would secure them even with his own greater hazard.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 ¶ Then the Philistines went up, and pitched in Judah <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Where the Rock <ns0:hi>Etam</ns0:hi> was, see 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 4. 32. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 5, 6.</ns0:note>, and spread themselves <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">As coming in great Numbers with a powerful Host.</ns0:note> in Lehi <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A place so called by anticipation, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:205" />10 And the men of Judah said, Why are ye come up against us? And they answered, To bind Samson are we come up, to do to him, as he hath done to us.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 Then three thousand men of Judah <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> went down.</ns0:note> went to the top of the rock Etam, and said to Samson, Knowest thou not that the Philistines <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> rulers over us? what <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou hast done unto us <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Thou hast by these actions punished not them, as thou intendedst; but us, who being under their Dominion, are sure to smart for it.</ns0:note>? And he said unto them, As they did unto me, so have I done unto them.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And they said unto him, We are come down to bind thee, that we may deliver thee into the hand of the Philistines. And Samson said unto them, Swear unto me, that ye will not fall upon me your selves <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Not that he feared them, or could not as easily have Conquered them, as he did the whole Host of the <ns0:hi>Phili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stines;</ns0:hi> but, because he would be free from all Obligation or Temptation of doing them any harm, though it were in his own just and necessary defence.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And they spake unto him, saying, No, but we will bind thee fast, and deliver thee into their hand: but surely we will not kill thee. And they bound him with two new cords, and brought him up from the rock <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From the Cave or Hole in the Rock, in which he had secured himself, out of which he was first brought up, and then carried down from the Rock to the Plain.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 ¶ And when he came unto Lehi, the Phili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stines shouted against him <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For Joy and Triumph, because they had now their great Enemy, as they supposed, in their hands.</ns0:note>, and the spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the cords that <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> upon his arms became as flax that was burnt with fire, and his bands <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> were melted.</ns0:note> loosed <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>were melt<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, i. e.</ns0:hi> were dissolved, as things are which are melted in the fire.</ns0:note> from off his hands.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And he found a <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> moist.</ns0:note> new <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">And therefore more tough and strong.</ns0:note> jaw-bone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And Samson said, With the jaw-bone of an ass, <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> an heap two heaps.</ns0:note> heaps upon heaps, with the jaw-bone of an ass have I slain a thousand men <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">This, though it might seem difficult, yet is not at all impossible or incredible; especially, seeing the Learned af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firm of the Asses of <ns0:hi>Syria,</ns0:hi> that they were larger and stron<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ger than ours, and so consequently were their Bones. And withal, it must be acknowledged, that there was something extraordinary and Miraculous in this, as there was unque<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stionably in <ns0:hi>Samson</ns0:hi>'s strength, and so all the difficulty va<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisheth.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And it came to pass, when<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he had made an end of speaking, that he cast away the jaw-bone out of his hand, and called that place <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>That is,</ns0:hi> the lifting up of the jaw-bone, or, casting a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />way of the jaw-bone.</ns0:note> Ramath-Lehi <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">And by contraction, <ns0:hi>Lehi,</ns0:hi> v. 14. it being usual so to con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tract Proper Names; as <ns0:hi>Salem</ns0:hi> is put for <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> Psal. 76. 3. <ns0:hi>Sheba</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>Beersheba, Ios.</ns0:hi> 19. 2. and many other.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 ¶ And he was sore athirst <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">So as he was ready to faint and die with Thirst; which was natural, from his excessive toil and heat; partly, sent by God, that by the experience of his own Impotency, he might be forced to ascribe the Victory to God onely, and not to himself.</ns0:note>, and called on the LORD, and said, Thou hast given this great deliverance into the hand of thy servant: and now shall I die for thirst, and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Wilt thou not finish what thou hast begun? Wilt thou undo what thou hast done.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 But God clave an hollow place <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> By cleaving a place, made it hollow; an expres<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion like that <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 47. 2. <ns0:hi>grind Meal, i. e.</ns0:hi> Grind Corn into Meal; and that <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 74. 15. <ns0:hi>thou didst cleave the Fountain, i. e.</ns0:hi> cleave the Rock so as to make a Fountain in it.</ns0:note> that was in <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Lehi.</ns0:note> the Jaw <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">In the Jaw-bone which he had used, which God could easily effect, either by causing the Jaw-bone to send forth Water, as the Rock formerly did, the Miracle being in effect the same, though in a differing subject, causing a Spring to break forth <ns0:hi>in Lehi,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>in that Le<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>i</ns0:hi> mention<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed before <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. for <ns0:hi>Lehi</ns0:hi> is both the name of a place, and signifies a <ns0:hi>Iaw-bone.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and there came water thereout, and when he had drunk, his spirit came again, and he revived: wherefore he called the name thereof <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>That is,</ns0:hi> the well of him that called, or, cried.</ns0:note> En-hakkore <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e. The Fountain of him that cryed</ns0:hi> for Thirst, or, <ns0:hi>that called</ns0:hi> upon God for Deliverance; <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> the Fountain or Well which was given in Answer to my Prayer.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in Lehi unto this day <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">According to this Translation, <ns0:hi>Lehi</ns0:hi> is the name of a place, and not a <ns0:hi>Iaw-bone,</ns0:hi> because it seems im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />probable that a Jaw-bone should continue there so long, which every Traveller might take away, and would be forward enough to carry a Fountain with them in those hot Countries; although it is not incredible that Passen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers would generally forbear to meddle with, or remove so great a Monument of Gods Power and Goodness; or, that the same God who made it instrumental to so great a wonder, should add one circumstance more, to wit, fix it in the earth, as a Testimony to Posterity of the Truth of this glorious work: But these words may be other<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wise rendred thus, <ns0:hi>which</ns0:hi> Fountain was <ns0:hi>in that Iaw-bone;</ns0:hi> and for the following words, <ns0:hi>unto this day;</ns0:hi> they may not be joined with the words next and immediately foregoing, as if the Fountain was there to this day; but with the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer words, <ns0:hi>he called,</ns0:hi> &c. and so the sense may be this, That it was so called unto this day, and the place may be thus read, <ns0:hi>he called the name thereof;</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>the name thereof was called</ns0:hi> (such active verbs being frequently put passively and impersonally,) <ns0:hi>The Well or Fountain of him that called</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>cryed (which</ns0:hi> was <ns0:hi>in Lehi) unto this day.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And he judged Israel <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He pleaded their Cause, and avenged them against the <ns0:hi>Philistinees.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> in the days of the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listines <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Whilst the <ns0:hi>Philistines</ns0:hi> had the Power and Dominion, from which he was not fully to deliver, but onely to <ns0:hi>begin to deliver</ns0:hi> them, as it was foretold, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 13. 5. From this place it is manifest that in the computation of the times of the Judges, the years of Servitude or Oppressi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on are not to be separated from the years of the Judges, and added to them, but are comprehended within them; which proposition is of great importance for clearing this difficult part of Scripture-Chronology, and for justifying that account of times given 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 6. 1.</ns0:note> twenty years.</ns0:p>
